topics.title: Introduction and Meaning of Dividend
explain: Dividend is the portion of Profit After Tax (PAT) distributed to shareholders.
Remaining profits are retained in the business as retained earnings for future growth.
Financial management covers financing, investment, and dividend decisions.
Ex-dividend price is the share trading price on the day after dividend declaration when rights expire.
topics.example: If a company earns ₹10 lakh PAT, it can distribute ₹4 lakh to owners as dividend and retain ₹6 lakh for factory expansion.
remember: Dividends can only be distributed out of Profit After Tax (PAT).
mistakes: Assuming ex-dividend buyers are entitled to receive the declared dividend.

quiz.q: What is the part of Profit After Tax (PAT) distributed to shareholders called?
quiz.why: Dividend is that portion of PAT which is paid out to company shareholders.

quiz.q: What happens to the share price on the ex-dividend date?
o: It trades excluding right to declared dividend
quiz.why: Ex-dividend refers to shares trading without the right to receive the declared dividend.

topics.title: Forms of Dividend
explain: Cash dividend is paid directly via cash, cheque, bank draft, or Electronic Clearing Service (ECS).
Share repurchases (buybacks) use corporate cash to buy back shares, which are then cancelled or kept as treasury shares.
Stock dividend (Bonus shares) involves issuing free additional shares to existing shareholders proportionately.
Bonus shares capitalise free reserves and increase share capital without altering overall net worth.
SEBI rules mandate that bonus shares cannot be issued in lieu of cash dividends.

flow.title: Modes of Dividend Payment
steps: Or Issue Bonus Shares from Free Reserves

topics.example: A 1:1 bonus issue gives 1 free share for every 1 share held, doubling share quantity while keeping proportional ownership unchanged.
remember: Bonus shares capitalise reserves and do not affect total net worth.
mistakes: Believing bonus shares increase the company's net worth or cash balance.

quiz.q: Which form of dividend capitalises free reserves without affecting company net worth?
quiz.why: Bonus shares convert retained earnings into equity capital without altering overall net worth.

quiz.q: According to SEBI rules, bonus shares CANNOT be issued:
quiz.why: SEBI explicitly prohibits companies from issuing bonus shares in place of cash dividends.

topics.title: Significance of Dividend Policy
explain: Dividend policy balances long-term financing needs with shareholder wealth maximisation.
Retained earnings serve as internal equity and incur zero floatation costs.
Distributing cash dividend reduces funds available for internal investment opportunities.
Shareholders often prefer current dividends due to market uncertainty and immediate income needs.

flow.title: Dividend Policy Decision Process
steps: Compare Project Return (ROI) with Equity Cost (Ke)

topics.example: A company with high-yielding projects retains more profits to save floatation costs of fresh equity issues.
remember: Retained earnings avoid floatation costs associated with issuing new equity shares.
mistakes: Ignoring shareholder preference for current income when planning profit retention.

quiz.q: Why are retained earnings preferred over fresh equity issues for financing investments?
quiz.why: Internal retained earnings do not incur issue expenses or floatation costs.

quiz.q: What does a wealth maximisation dividend decision balance?
quiz.why: Management must divide earnings between dividends and retention to maximize shareholder wealth.

topics.title: Relationship Between Retained Earnings and Growth
explain: Growth rate of a firm depends on retention ratio and internal return on investment.
The fundamental growth equation is Growth (g) = b x r.
Here 'b' represents retention ratio (1 - payout ratio) and 'r' represents rate of return on investment.
If a firm pays out 100% earnings as dividend (b = 0), its growth rate becomes zero.

flow.title: How Retained Earnings Drive Growth
steps: Achieve Firm Growth (g = b x r)

topics.example: If a firm retains 60% of earnings (b = 0.6) and earns a 15% return on investment (r = 0.15), growth rate g = 0.6 x 15% = 9%.
remember: Growth formula: g = b x r.
mistakes: Using dividend payout ratio instead of retention ratio (b) in the growth formula.

quiz.q: In the equation g = br, what does 'b' stand for?
quiz.why: 'b' represents the retention ratio, which is the fraction of earnings retained in the business.

quiz.q: If a company retains 40% of profits and earns 20% ROI, what is its growth rate?
quiz.why: Growth g = b x r = 0.40 x 20% = 8%.

topics.title: Determinants of Dividend Decisions
explain: Dividend decisions depend on funds availability, cost of capital, capital structure, and shareholder expectations.
Under Section 123 of Companies Act 2013, dividends can be declared from current profits after depreciation or previous undistributed profits.
Unrealised gains, notional gains, or fixed asset revaluation gains cannot be used for dividend payment.
Finance Act 2020 abolished Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) on companies; dividends are now taxed in the hands of investors under 'Other income'.
topics.example: A company earning profit cannot pay dividend out of revaluation reserve created by revaluing its factory land.
remember: Dividends received on or after 1st April 2020 are taxable in the hands of shareholders.
mistakes: Assuming Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) is still payable by the company.

quiz.q: Under Section 123 of Companies Act 2013, dividends must be declared after providing for:
quiz.why: Section 123 requires profits to be computed after providing for depreciation before declaring dividends.

quiz.q: How is dividend income taxed after the amendment by Finance Act 2020?
o: Taxable in hands of company as DDT
Taxable in hands of investor under 'Other income'
quiz.why: Finance Act 2020 made dividends taxable directly in the hands of the receiving shareholder.

topics.title: Practical Considerations and Payout Policies
explain: Mature companies with limited investment options maintain high payout ratios, while growth companies retain most profits.
Constant dividend policy pays a fixed rupee dividend per share using a Dividend Equalisation Reserve in lean years.
Stable dividend policy maintains a fixed percentage payout ratio on net earnings every year.
Lintner's model states current dividends depend on current earnings and previous year's dividend.
Lintner's formula: D1 = D0 + [(EPS x Target payout) - D0] x Af, where Af is the adjustment factor.

flow.title: Lintner's Dividend Adjustment Model
steps: Add to Previous Dividend (D0) for D1

topics.example: Infosys declared a policy to distribute up to 30% of Consolidated Profit After Tax (PAT) as dividend every year.
remember: Lintner's formula: D1 = D0 + [(EPS x Target Payout) - D0] x Af.
mistakes: Confusing constant dividend per share policy with constant dividend payout ratio policy.

quiz.q: Which dividend policy maintains a fixed percentage payout on annual net earnings?
quiz.why: Stable dividend policy pays a fixed percentage on net earnings each year.

quiz.q: In Lintner's model, what does parameter 'Af' represent?
o: Adjustment factor or speed of adjustment
quiz.why: 'Af' stands for the adjustment factor or speed at which dividends adjust toward the target payout.

topics.title: Dividend Irrelevance: MM Hypothesis
explain: Modigliani-Miller (MM) hypothesis proves dividend policy has no effect on firm value or stock price in perfect markets.
Firm value depends solely on earning power and investment policy, not on profit distribution.
Paying cash dividend reduces firm cash, requiring fresh equity issue which causes capital loss balancing the dividend gain.
MM formula for share price at year start: P0 = (P1 + D1) / (1 + Ke).
MM formula for total firm value: nP0 = [(n + Delta-n)P1 - I + E] / (1 + Ke).

flow.title: MM Arbitrage Process
steps: Share Price Drops by Dividend Amount
Issue Delta-n New Shares at P1
Total Value of Firm (nP0) Remains Unchanged

topics.example: If a share priced at ₹100 pays ₹5 dividend, its price drops to ₹95 ex-dividend; investor total wealth stays ₹100.
remember: MM Model Formula: P0 = (P1 + D1) / (1 + Ke).
mistakes: Applying MM hypothesis in real-world scenarios where taxes or transaction costs exist.

quiz.q: According to Modigliani and Miller (MM) hypothesis, firm value depends on:
quiz.why: MM states firm value depends entirely on its earning power and investment decisions, not dividend payout.

quiz.q: Under MM hypothesis, what is the formula to calculate opening share price P0?
quiz.why: MM formula rearranges to P0 = (P1 + D1) / (1 + Ke).

topics.title: Dividend Relevance: Walter's Model
explain: James E. Walter argues dividend policy directly affects market price of share based on 'r' (return) vs 'Ke' (cost of equity).
Walter's formula: Market Price P = [D + (r / Ke)(E - D)] / Ke.
For Growth firms (r > Ke): Optimal payout ratio is 0% (retain all profits to maximize share price).
For Declining firms (r < Ke): Optimal payout ratio is 100% (distribute all profits to shareholders).
For Normal firms (r = Ke): Dividend policy has no effect on share price; every payout ratio is optimal.

flow.title: Walter's Model Decision Logic
steps: Calculate Internal Return (r) and Cost of Equity (Ke)
If r > Ke: Set Dividend Payout to 0%
If r < Ke: Set Dividend Payout to 100%
Compute Stock Price P = [D + (r/Ke)(E - D)] / Ke

remember: Walter's Formula: P = [D + (r / Ke)(E - D)] / Ke.
mistakes: Plugging total company earnings instead of per-share values (EPS and DPS) into Walter's formula.

quiz.q: What is the optimal dividend payout ratio for a growth firm (r > Ke) under Walter's model?
quiz.why: When r > Ke, retaining all earnings (0% payout) yields the highest market price per share.

quiz.q: What happens to stock price in Walter's model when r = Ke?
o: Remains unaffected by dividend payout ratio
quiz.why: When return equals cost of capital, every payout ratio gives the same share price.

topics.title: Dividend Relevance: Gordon's Model and DDM
explain: Myron Gordon states dividends are relevant due to investor risk aversion (Bird-in-hand theory).
Investors prefer certainty of current dividends over uncertainty of future capital gains.
Gordon's model formula: P0 = E1(1 - b) / (Ke - br) or P0 = D1 / (Ke - g), where g = br.
For growth firms (r > Ke), share price increases as retention ratio increases (payout decreases).
Dividend Discount Model (DDM) values stock as the present value of all expected future dividends plus PV of final sale price.

flow.title: Valuation using Gordon's Growth Model
steps: Identify Retention Ratio (b) and Payout Ratio (1 - b)
Compute Growth Rate g = b x r

remember: Gordon's Model requires Ke > g for a valid positive valuation.
mistakes: Using past dividend D0 instead of expected future dividend D1 in the Gordon formula numerator.

quiz.q: What is the underlying concept of Gordon's Revised Model?
quiz.why: Gordon's revised model relies on the Bird-in-hand theory, assuming investors prefer current cash dividends to risky future capital gains.

quiz.q: In Gordon's formula P0 = D1 / (Ke - g), what is the condition required for validity?
quiz.why: Ke must be strictly greater than g to ensure a finite and positive stock price.

topics.title: Stock Splits and Share Buyback
explain: Stock split divides existing shares into a higher number of shares with lower face value.
Stock splits lower unit share price, making shares affordable to small retail investors and improving liquidity.
Stock splits do not alter total share capital or net worth, but reduce face value per share.
Share buyback repurchases company shares from the open market or tender offer using corporate cash.
Bought-back shares are cancelled, reducing circulating shares and boosting future EPS and market price.

flow.title: Execution of Stock Split vs Buyback
steps: For Stock Split: Subdivide Face Value & Increase Share Count
For Buyback: Repurchase & Cancel Shares using Cash
Reduce Outstanding Share Count in Buyback
Increase Future EPS and Market Value

topics.example: Splitting 1 share of ₹500 face value into 5 shares of ₹100 face value reduces market price to enhance trading liquidity.
remember: Stock splits change the face value of shares; bonus issues do not change face value.
mistakes: Confusing stock splits with bonus shares; splits reduce face value, whereas bonus issues keep face value unchanged.

quiz.q: What happens to the face value of a share during a stock split?
quiz.why: A stock split divides the face value into smaller denominations proportionately.

quiz.q: What is the primary effect of a share buyback on outstanding equity shares?
o: Reduces outstanding shares and increases future EPS
quiz.why: Buyback cancels repurchased shares, reducing total outstanding shares and increasing future EPS.
